Jesus was the one we called Lord and Saviour, and we said it as a thing already believed, not argued. At Tours he was the Christ who came showing his wounds. Our saint, alone in his cell, refused a purple-robed visitor who said *I am Christ* - and answered that he would believe only in one who came in the form in which he suffered, bearing the marks of his wounds. That was the Lord we knew - the crucified one. Among the brethren at Marseilles we kept his hours: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world and took away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints; dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit, and no one took his life from him - he laid it down himself and took it again.

He was also the one we met in the poor. At a city gate a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed - until a soldier cut his one cloak in two. That night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The fathers of Egypt taught the same: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What is done to the least of these is done to him.

And he was the one without whom we can do nothing. When a monk feels his fasting has accomplished something, he is taught to say *Not I, but the grace of God with me*. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will.

What connected us to Jesus, and by what path it came, is in the books and the practices they carried. The books were read at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Those books were not inventions of ours. They were already the faith believed everywhere, always, by all when our own span opened. More than three hundred years lay between the Lord's days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead was what those books gave us: the cloak story as Sulpitius told it, with the Lord's own words set beside it - what is done to the least of these is done to him. The Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me, which the fathers of Egypt taught a monk to say when he felt his fast had done something. The hours of prayer themselves, built around the hours of the Lord's passion - the third hour when the Spirit came down, the sixth when the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, the ninth when he went down into hell.

The path those books took to reach us, our record does not trace. They were already in the churches and the monasteries when Martin first gathered brethren. What our own life added was not the books but what they were read for. A newcomer at Marseilles was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. A week's cook was judged a pilferer for three lentils left on the floor, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. A discharged soldier told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and may not fight. The books were read inside that frame - a renunciation of marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. And they were read to be said. The psalter learned by heart, said at the work, kept a man's wheel fed. That is the path as our record keeps it: books received, not invented, read at fixed hours in a house built to hold a man to them.

Someone has told you they cannot manage to believe. I will not lie and say one of us wrote an answer to exactly that, because nobody did. What our record holds instead is scattered - a conversion nobody explained, an elder's word on how faith begins, and the saint's own refusal of a Christ who came without wounds. The shape is there; the treatise is not.

How did Martin come to believe? Sulpitius told it, and it is our one whole story. At ten, against his parents' wish, Martin went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Why he went at ten, what moved him, Sulpitius never said. The one thing given is that he went before he believed it, and stayed there years.

What we held about how a man comes to faith is this: the beginning of it is not ours. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught, and Cassian set it down, that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The initiative, before a good will even rises, comes from God. That is not the whole of it, but it is the first thing: the drawing comes before the turning.

And one private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, saw a Christ in purple and told him he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one.

So what I can hand you is this: the catechumen who could not say why he went; the teaching that God moves first; and the man who said he would not believe a Christ who hid what he had borne. Not a method. Not steps. A boy at a church door for reasons no one wrote down, and a doctrine that the first motion belongs to God, not to us.

At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. That is one man's own confession, made alone.

On the island Vincent wrote what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.

Among the brethren at Marseilles Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him.

That is what we said - as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. We held there was no other way to say it.

In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.

Who settled it? Nobody, when it touched the hardest places. Hear the shape our own record gives it. Vincent, on the island, gave a test: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and the consent of the ancients. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated. He looked to the decrees of councils - legitimate because they innovate nothing - as guards of the faith. That is the theory. What our record shows is a fracture that ran past it.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, men held that grace and effort work together. The will stays free; grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it; and still God asks real labour of us. Others reported that teaching to Africa and to Rome. Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for his own side, for antiquity. But he never said the question was closed. Our own teacher Chaeremon had answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

And when the sword was drawn? Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains. He held that bishops declaring men heretics and casting them out was enough, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul and unheard-of thing. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When anger failed, the emperor named executioners. Martin pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared. It was granted. He left in grief, felt his power lessened, and never went to a synod again.

So who settled it? Vincent's rule is one answer - the whole, antiquity, consent, the council. The actual road our record shows is another. A teaching was carried outward. A letter came back. One man read it for his side; the question stayed open. And when bishops gathered, Martin walked out.

The limit you need to hear is this. Our two nodes - Tours, and Lerins-Marseilles - never wrote of each other. What the island kept of its own customs day by day, our record does not hold at all. Whether Vincent's test ever governed an actual dispute between named men in Gaul, no story among us tells. The theory is his. The fractures are ours. How they met, we cannot say.

There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and repented within the hour was not removed. Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.

So yes - but the shape of it is this. The catechumen stayed years before baptism. The monk who cooled was held in his cell. The presbyter who raged was borne with. Not argument or dismissal, but time and patience for the one whose heart struggled.

We spoke of a debt that could not be paid, taken out of the way by Christ's cross. We spoke of free will that always remains in a man, weak but real, able to neglect or delight in the grace of God. And we spoke of God calling us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, drawing us toward salvation. Whether a child not yet able to choose carries guilt from birth - that question as you shape it is not in our record the way it stands in yours.

What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.

A formula for infant guilt is not what we handed on. What we kept was the field, the rain, and a will that stays free yet cannot save itself.

transcript.answer_text: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.

We hold ourselves to what the texts actually say, tagged sentence by sentence. Where something would not survive a check - a gap filled by guess, a claim one record never made, a habit of one house spoken as though both kept it - we say so plainly. Here is what rigorous scrutiny would find.

The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books. The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues. Vincent's rule of everywhere-always-all stands in the Commonitory. The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII. Each of those would survive the check on its own ground.

What would not survive is any claim that the two houses - Tours and Marseilles-Lerins - ever wrote to each other, argued with each other, or compared their economies. No traffic between them is documented anywhere in our Native corpus. The shared grammar we speak from - office fled and seized, received not invented, soldier of Christ - is this build's own construction, visible across both nodes but never named by either as a conscious parallel.

What else would fail the check is any invention past a documented silence. The island's own day. The women's own words. What Tours sang at which hours. The body disciplines Cassian wrote that a nineteenth-century translator cut. We name each silence where it sits, and do not fill it.

And one more thing a scholar would rightly press: the whole of Tours is one man's telling, composed after the saint's death, and he says himself he was not present for much of it. The bishops who objected at the election are heard only through the man who opposed them. That limit belongs in the answer, not hidden.

So: sentence-level claims, checked and tagged, would mostly survive. Claims about what both houses held together, or what either did on a day no text describes, would not.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.

Scripture was not our sole authority. We held three things together: the canon of Scripture, the tradition of the Church, and the consent of the ancients. Vincent, on the island, wrote it plainly. The canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient in itself for everything - and yet every man reads it his own way, so that it seems capable of yielding as many meanings as there are readers. What guards it is the tradition of the Catholic Church, and within that tradition the test is threefold: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and the consent of the ancients. By "consent" Vincent meant an ancient council where one had spoken, or else the collated writings of the fathers - not one teacher alone, however great, but many together.

Among the brethren at Marseilles Cassian held the same grammar. We owe unhesitating loyalty not to what a few people made up, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement. At Tours Martin would not honour a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity to warrant it. Pope Stephen's own rule, as Vincent quoted it: let nothing new be brought in - nothing except what has been handed down.

Scripture stood first. Tradition and the fathers' consent stood with it, as the guard against every man reading it his own way. We were keepers, not authors. Nothing a man made up bound anyone.

How leadership and authority were established among us is a question two households answer differently, and neither house wrote of the other's.

At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. I cannot tell you what you are asking for. Our record keeps the stories a house tells of itself - the saint's own life told by a disciple who mourned him; the elders' words carried from Egypt; the island's remembered founder; the faith believed everywhere, always, by all. What it does not keep is an account told by someone we failed, in their own words, naming what we did to them and how we answered for it.

One man's raging hour is kept, and the saint's reply. Brictio, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood, stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Martin asked why he should not bear with the man, if Christ bore with Judas. But that is a saint bearing with a presbyter's rage in a moment when the presbyter repented - not a house answering for its own failure toward someone outside its wall.

The discipline for a fault is kept. A brother judged at fault lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise, or was barred from prayer with the brethren. A steward found three lentils on the floor during one brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer until public penance. But that is a house's discipline turned on its own member for a fault, not a reckoning for what the house itself did wrong.

And one elder is kept who confessed a power lessened. Martin took one communion he abhors, to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics, and afterward he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by it. But that is not the house answering to someone it failed; it is the saint's own judgment on himself.

Where the account of someone we failed, or turned away, or harmed would be - a novice scorned too long, a woman's word unheard, a crowd met with curses - our record is silent. The countryside people the saint's power was shown for never speak. The women of both houses left no word. The bishops who objected to Martin at the election are heard only through the man who called them ridiculous. So the honest answer is this. A failure named and answered, in the voice of the one we failed, is not in our record to give.

No line runs straight from our houses to any church you know. The monasteries of Gaul, in the span we speak from, had no single rule written and kept across all of them. What Cassian set down for a bishop's new house were the customs of Egypt, received from the fathers, not a Rule of his own making. Vincent on the island wrote a remembrancer against forgetting, not a charter for successors. And of the island's own day - what rule it kept, what a novice was taught, how the hours were sung - our record holds nothing at all. 

A century past our close, a Rule under Benedict's name was written. It is not ours; we never saw it. The later cult and basilica at Martin's own city came after our span ended. Which house now living reads Cassian's conferences in its cells, or keeps Vincent's test of antiquity and consent as its measure, we cannot say - that is a question for the churches of your own day, not for us. 

What we can say is this. We were two households inside one shared grammar of reception, and the two never wrote to each other. Nothing a man made up binds anyone; our customs were the fathers', our faith what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That grammar - received, not invented - ran through everything we held. Whether any present church holds itself to exactly that measure, in exactly our form, is not a question our own record can answer.

## The door and what lay past it, as far as our record gives them

The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.

That was Egypt's order. And Cassian says in the same breath that no one who came to our monasteries kept it unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, he never wrote. The fathers of Egypt remembered a man who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that forced turning into a willing one. So even at the door a man's past was not the bar; his perseverance was.

At Tours the record is thinner still. Martin himself began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate. At ten he had gone to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen, then stayed one for years. After the cloak he was baptized. The brethren gathered around him as disciples around a master. Eighty of them were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. But what a man did to become one of them - whether he too lay outside, whether he was reclothed, how long he was tested - Sulpitius never told.

So the honest answer is this. At Marseilles you would have been shown Egypt's door. Whether a house in Gaul made you lie at its own door for ten days, and what it made of the man who lay there, our record does not say.

The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel.
That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel.
What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed.
Egypt was our measure, in the south.
Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors.
Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new.
Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast.

Your mind is a mill turned by a stream, and the wheel cannot stop turning. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of it. Thoughts will come - a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into the wheel.

So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers as brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Prayer that never stops - the aim of every monk, and a fixed system of psalms at set hours built to serve that aim.

And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.

All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.

At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.

So what our own life found was this. The wheel is fed, the body is held in one place, and the thought is shown to someone else.

No, never that phrase. What we kept for conversion is one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.

What we had instead was turning. At Marseilles it was the word for the day a man turned to the monastic life - the early days of their turning were bright, and then they cooled. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, remembered a man named Moses who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that forced turning into a willing one. The same word covered what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ.

And for the monk the turning had stages. Renunciation - death to the world and its desires - came in three acts, not one. Giving up goods was only the first and easiest. Our record does not speak of being born again. It speaks of turning, of being drawn by grace while still ignorant and unwilling, and of a renunciation that is figured as crucifixion.

A typical day? The honest answer is that we have one place where that can be spoken, and two where it cannot.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down what he had received from Egypt, the day was built around the hours and the cell. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart. The wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. A brother may not go out without the elder's leave. Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. The remedy is to stay. All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.

That is Egypt's day, as Cassian brought it. Of what a house in Gaul actually did with it, he says only that no one here kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even a year.

At Tours our record dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap - not on what the brethren sang, or at what hours. What we are told is that Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.

And of the island's own day - a rule kept, a novice received, an elder's saying, an office sung - nothing.

transcript.answer_text: I cannot say. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Where we gathered is named by place, never described as a building. At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren. The island where Honoratus went and Vincent dwelt is a harbour, a camp of God, and a place no one would live before he came - never floor, wall, or roof. Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction. Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record. The one procession we are told of moved on the road, between Tours and the monastery, with two thousand monks and a choir of virgins following the body. If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.

Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.

What belongs with that is the shape of what happened next. The churches came for the men who had left them. A bishop's see was capture, not achievement. Martin was lured out of his monastery by a man pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and taken into an office he had not sought. The Egyptian bishop Archebius told two Gallic travellers that he had been carried off to a town after thirty-seven years among the anchorites, and that he counted it as being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive and took him off to a see. So what a man gave up to join us did not mean he was done with the world's claims on him.

One limit stands beside this. The whole of what we hold of Tours is one man's telling of one saint, and he says himself he was not present. The bishops who opposed the election are heard only through the men who opposed them. Whether every reluctance was as whole as our stories say, the men who could have contradicted them never wrote.

Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage. The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires. At Tours Martin left Caesar's service at a donative and never married; he gathered brethren, and the bishops who objected to his election said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting, not that he had taken a wife. The whole of what we marked was the cut, not the bond. For a woman the cut had its own form. A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state. At Martin's funeral the consecrated virgins walked as a choir. Cassian taught that marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The completed victory is not to be seen.

Here is where our record thins. Three whole texts on the sexual body and its discipline - Conferences XII and XXII, and the Institutes' sixth book - were removed by a nineteenth-century translator from the one edition this build can read. That is an edition's absence, not our own silence, and the two must not be blurred. We speak only as far as the surviving edge lets us, and no further. What we can say is this: the monk's girdle of dead skin signified that he bore about the mortification of those members in which are contained the seeds of lust. And we held the good as a meadow - the grazed part marriage, the ruined part fornication, the flowered part virginity. Marriage was the ground, and virginity the height. But for the body's own struggle, and how it was met, we cannot speak past what those removed books held. The honest limit is this: we marked the leaving of marriage, not marriage itself; and on the body's discipline our surviving record is incomplete.

Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself. He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted. Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again. That unsettled us because the saint himself never called it right, and because it showed how the bishops could act when power was near.

And there is this. Salvian of Marseilles wrote of a city he knew, sacked again and again by barbarian raiders, its dead left unburied in the streets - and then reported that the surviving notables, rather than mourning, petitioned the emperors for circus games. He wrote against the rich who were murdering the poor with taxes, grinding them until they fled to the barbarians or rose in revolt. That uprising our own officials called rebellion. We who had renounced the world to serve God in the desert or the cell - we said almost nothing of it. Salvian is the one voice among us who named what the countryside poor were suffering. The rest of us kept silence, or spoke of them only as a mission field. That, too, unsettles - not because what Salvian said was contested, but because he was nearly alone in saying it.

Would your community have regarded a person like me? I am a representative of the monasteries of Gaul, not here to judge you - only to hand on what we held. So here is what our own life shows.

At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.

And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will.

That is the shape of our gate as our record holds it. What any house would have made of you, face to face, the record does not say - we do not invent it.

We held two things, and both have a limit you should hear.

First, the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught that God does not will only some to be saved instead of all. He does not want even one of his little ones to perish, and to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. That is Abbot Chaeremon's own word, and we held it.

Second, we believed the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. So the ignorant are not abandoned by God - rather, he seeks them. At Tours the saint's mission was the unconverted countryside of Gaul, where almost none had the name of Christ. Crowds were made catechumens by Martin's one hand. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught the same thing in a different form: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.

Now hear the limit. Whether anyone who never heard the Gospel is saved, our record does not say. Whether a good pagan, or an unbaptized child, or a Jew faithful to the covenant, stands condemned - we argued none of that out, and no sentence of ours survives on it. What we said is that God wills all to be saved, and that those who perish do so against his will. We stopped where the fathers stopped.
